theory_refs.at: Overlapping queries re-add the same elements

theory_refs.why: The boundary picture that kills off-by-ones.

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ Design a class: constructor gets an array; `sumRange(l, r)` returns a[l] + … + a[r] (inclusive). Up to 10⁴ queries on n ≤ 10⁴.
- The array never changes ("immutable").

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Per-query loop: 10⁴ queries × 10⁴ length = 10⁸ — borderline. The real point: many queries on a static array.
✍️ By hand: sum(2..4) = (sum of first 5) − (sum of first 2). If I had all "sum of first i", every query is one subtraction.
✍️ Edges: l = 0 (must not read index −1); l == r.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** Loop from l to r per query. O(n) per query.
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: different queries re-add overlapping elements.
✍️ ↳ Unlock: "recomputing something…" → precompute every running total once.
✍️ **2. Optimal.** Build `pre` in O(n); answer each query as `pre[r+1] − pre[l]` in O(1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. In the constructor, build pre of size n+1 with pre[0] = 0 and pre[i+1] = pre[i] + a[i].
✍️ 2. For a query (l, r), return pre[r+1] − pre[l].

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
CONSTRUCT  pre = [0] * (n+1)
           for i in 0..n-1: pre[i+1] = pre[i] + a[i]
QUERY      return pre[r+1] - pre[l]
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ Build O(n), query O(1), space O(n).
✍️ The leading 0 means l = 0 needs no special case.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ Many range-sum queries on a static array → prefix sums.
✍️ `pre[k]` = sum of the first k elements = boundary before index k.
✍️ Sum of a[l..r] = pre[r+1] − pre[l]. Memorise the picture, not the formula.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *The array gets point updates between queries.* Fenwick tree / segment tree: O(log n) update and query (beyond this plan; mention it).
- *2D version.* Rectangle sums with inclusion–exclusion ([[ps-2d-prefix-sum]]).

siblings.title: Product of Array Except Self
siblings.maps: Prefix and suffix **products** instead of sums; division is banned, so combine a left pass and a right pass.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ out[i] = product of all elements except a[i]; O(n), no division.
✍️ Division would break on zeros anyway.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Brute: for each i multiply the rest → O(n²). out[i] = (product of a[0..i−1]) × (product of a[i+1..n−1]) → a forward pass and a backward pass. Write the forward pass into out, then sweep backwards with one variable → O(1) extra.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Pass 1: out[i] = product of everything left of i. Pass 2 from the right: multiply out[i] by a running product of everything right of i.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
out[0] = 1
for i in 1..n-1: out[i] = out[i-1] * a[i-1]
right = 1
for i from n-1 down to 0: out[i] *= right; right *= a[i]
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ "Everything except me" = left part ⊕ right part ([[ps-prefix-suffix-passes#idea]]); zeros need no special case ([[ps-prefix-suffix-passes#why-no-division]]).

siblings.title: Range Sum Query 2D - Immutable
siblings.maps: The same idea in two dimensions with inclusion–exclusion.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Many queries for the sum of a sub-rectangle of a static matrix.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Per-query double loop → O(R·C) per query. 2D prefix P[r+1][c+1] = sum of rectangle (0,0)..(r,c) → O(1) per query.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Build P with "add up, add left, subtract the overlap"; answer with four lookups.

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Inclusion–exclusion in both the build and the query ([[ps-2d-prefix-sum#query]]).

siblings.title: Find the Highest Altitude
siblings.maps: The answer is just the maximum prefix sum (including the starting 0).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Start at altitude 0; gain[i] is the change; return the highest altitude reached.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Running sum + running max, starting the max at 0.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Add each gain to the altitude; track the maximum.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
alt = 0; best = 0
for g in gain: alt += g; best = max(best, alt)
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ The starting point (prefix of length 0) is a real candidate — the same reason the prefix array starts with 0.

theory_refs.why: Why a window cannot work here.
The bottleneck that becomes a lookup.
Avoid counting empty subarrays when k = 0.

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(array of ints, possibly negative; k) → number of contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k.
- n ≤ 2·10⁴, values in [−1000, 1000], k in [−10⁷, 10⁷].
- [1, 1, 1], k = 2 → 2. [1, 2, 3], k = 3 → 2 ([1,2] and [3]).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ "Subarray sum" + negatives → not a window. "Count" + "exactly k" → think prefix sums.
✍️ By hand: sum(i..j) = pre[j+1] − pre[i]. For a fixed end, I want starts whose prefix equals (current prefix − k).
✍️ Hard part: counting **all** such starts quickly, and not missing subarrays that start at 0.
✍️ Edges: k = 0; negative values; a single element equal to k.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** All (i, j) with an inner sum loop. O(n³).
✍️ **2. Better.** Fix i, extend j with a running sum. O(n²) — 4·10⁸, too slow in practice.
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: for each end, trying every start.
✍️ ↳ Job description: "count earlier prefix sums equal to run − k". Unlock: searching for a known value → store prefix sums in a map with their counts.
✍️ **3. Optimal.** One pass; `cnt[prefix] = how many times seen`; add cnt[run − k] at each step. O(n) time, O(n) space.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Keep a running prefix sum, starting at 0, and a map of prefix counts containing {0: 1}.
✍️ 2. For each element, add it to the running sum.
✍️ 3. Add the number of earlier prefixes equal to (running − k) to the answer.
✍️ 4. Record the current running sum in the map.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   cnt = map {0: 1}; run = 0; ans = 0
LOOP    for x in a
UPDATE    run += x
CHECK     ans += cnt[run - k]        (query first, using find)
UPDATE    cnt[run] += 1              (record after)
RETURN  ans
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) average time, O(n) space.
✍️ Without the {0: 1} seed, [3] with k = 3 returns 0.
✍️ Recording before querying with k = 0 counts each position as a zero-length subarray.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ Subarray sum = k (or divisible by k, or balanced counts) → prefix sum + hash map.
✍️ It is Two Sum where the "values" are prefix sums: store what you have seen, look up run − k.
✍️ Negatives allowed → do not use a sliding window.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Longest subarray with sum k.* Map prefix → first index, seed {0: −1} ([[ps-prefix-sum-hashmap#variations]]).
- *Sum divisible by k.* Key by `run mod k`, normalised ([[ps-modular-prefix]]).
- *All values positive?* Then a sliding window also works in O(1) space.

siblings.title: Subarray Sums Divisible by K
siblings.maps: Same counting map, but keyed by the prefix sum's remainder mod k.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Count subarrays whose sum is divisible by k. Values can be negative.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ sum(i..j) divisible ⇔ pre[j+1] ≡ pre[i] (mod k). Count equal remainders with an array of size k seeded with count[0] = 1. Normalise negative remainders.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ For each element: update the running remainder; add how many earlier prefixes had the same remainder; record it.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
cnt[k] = 0; cnt[0] = 1; run = 0; ans = 0
for x in a:
    run = ((run + x) % k + k) % k
    ans += cnt[run]; cnt[run]++
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Equal remainders bound a divisible subarray ([[ps-modular-prefix#idea]]); C++ `%` can be negative ([[ps-modular-prefix#negative-mod]]).

siblings.title: Contiguous Array
siblings.maps: Turn 0 into −1; equal 0s and 1s means sum 0; find the longest such subarray with a first-index map.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Longest subarray of a binary array with equally many 0s and 1s.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Map 0 → −1. Then "equal counts" = "sum 0". Longest subarray with sum 0: two equal prefix sums; store the **first** index of each prefix value, seed {0: −1}.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Running sum with ±1; if this sum was seen, length = i − first[sum]; otherwise record first[sum] = i.

stages.title: Pseudocode
Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ "Longest" → store the **first** occurrence (never overwrite); "count" → store counts ([[ps-prefix-sum-hashmap#variations]]).

siblings.title: Binary Subarrays With Sum
siblings.maps: Exactly Subarray Sum Equals K on a 0/1 array (the window alternative is atMost(goal) − atMost(goal−1)).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Count subarrays of a binary array with sum equal to goal.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Prefix + count map, identical template. Alternative: because values are ≥ 0, sliding windows work with the at-most trick ([[sw-at-most-k-trick#idea]]).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Running sum; add cnt[run − goal]; record run.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
cnt = {0:1}; run = 0; ans = 0
for x in a: run += x; ans += cnt[run-goal]; cnt[run]++
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ When prefix values are small and non-negative, an array replaces the hash map ([[cpp-container-choice#rule]]).

theory_refs.at: For a fixed end, the best start comes from the previous end
theory_refs.why: How Kadane falls out of the bottleneck method.
What to say when asked why it is correct.
"Best ending at i" is a DP state you will see again on Day 25.

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(array, possibly negative) → the largest sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray.
- n ≤ 10⁵ → O(n) or O(n log n).
- [−2,1,−3,4,−1,2,1,−5,4] → 6 ([4,−1,2,1]).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ By hand: I keep adding while the total helps. When the running total becomes negative it can only drag down anything after it, so I start fresh.
✍️ Hard part: the all-negative case — the answer is the single largest element, not 0.
✍️ Edges: n = 1; all negative; zeros.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** All (i, j), sum each. O(n³), or O(n²) with running sums.
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: for each end j, trying every start i.
✍️ ↳ Observation: the best subarray ending at j is either [a[j]] alone or (best subarray ending at j−1) + a[j]. So "best ending at j" comes from "best ending at j−1" in O(1).
✍️ **2. Optimal (Kadane).** cur = max(a[j], cur + a[j]); best = max(best, cur). O(n), O(1).
✍️ (Prefix-sum view: answer = max over j of pre[j+1] − min prefix before it — the same as tomorrow's stock problem.)

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Set cur and best to the first element.
✍️ 2. For each next element: cur becomes the larger of (the element alone) and (cur plus the element).
✍️ 3. Update best with cur.
✍️ 4. Return best.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   cur = a[0]; best = a[0]
LOOP    for i in 1..n-1
UPDATE    cur  = max(a[i], cur + a[i])     extend or restart
          best = max(best, cur)
RETURN  best
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) time, O(1) space.
✍️ All negative [−3, −1, −2] → −1. `best = 0` initialisation would wrongly return 0.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ "Best contiguous segment" → state = best ending exactly here; extend or restart.
✍️ This is the first DP of the plan: dp[i] depends only on dp[i−1].
✍️ Initialise optimisation answers with the first real candidate, not with 0.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Return the subarray.* Track the start index at each restart and the best (start, end).
- *Divide and conquer version* (LeetCode's follow-up): best of left half, right half, and crossing the middle → O(n log n).
- *Circular array.* max(Kadane, total − min subarray), unless all negative ([[kad-kadane#variations]]).
- *Maximum product.* Track max and min ([[kad-max-product-variant]]).

siblings.title: Maximum Product Subarray
siblings.maps: Kadane with products — but a negative turns the minimum into the maximum, so track both.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Largest product of a contiguous subarray; values in [−10, 10] including 0.
✍️ Why plain Kadane fails: [−2, 3, −4] → the best is the whole array (24), built from a very negative product times −4.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Keep hi and lo = max and min product ending here. For x < 0 swap them first; then hi = max(x, hi·x), lo = min(x, lo·x). O(n).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ For each x: if negative, swap hi/lo; update both from the old values; best = max(best, hi).

stages.title: Pseudocode
Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ When an operation can flip order (negatives, multiplication), keep both extremes ([[kad-max-product-variant#idea]]).

siblings.title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
siblings.maps: A wrapping subarray = total minus a middle subarray → max(Kadane max, total − Kadane min).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Max subarray sum when the array is circular (a subarray may wrap from the end to the start).

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Either the best subarray does not wrap (normal Kadane) or it wraps, in which case the excluded part is a contiguous middle block with minimum sum. If every value is negative, the wrap case would be empty → use normal Kadane.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Run max-Kadane and min-Kadane together with the total; answer as above.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
compute maxSub, minSub, total
if maxSub < 0: return maxSub
return max(maxSub, total - minSub)
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Complement trick: "maximum wrapping part" = "total − minimum non-wrapping part".

siblings.title: Maximum Absolute Sum of Any Subarray
siblings.maps: Run Kadane for the max and for the min; the answer is the bigger magnitude.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Maximum of |sum| over all subarrays (empty allowed → at least 0).

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ |sum| is largest either at the max subarray sum or at the min subarray sum → two Kadanes in one pass.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Track max-ending-here (floored at 0) and min-ending-here (capped at 0); answer = max(best max, −best min).

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
hi = lo = 0; ans = 0
for x: hi = max(0, hi + x); lo = min(0, lo + x); ans = max(ans, hi, -lo)
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Allowing an empty subarray lets you floor the running value at 0 (classic Kadane variant).

theory_refs.at: For each sell day, the best buy is the minimum before it
Profit first, then fold today into the minimum
theory_refs.why: The order of the two updates.
Day 29 extends this to cooldowns, fees and k transactions.
Kadane on daily differences gives the same answer.

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(prices by day) → max of prices[j] − prices[i] with i < j, or 0 if no profit is possible. One buy, one sell.
- n ≤ 10⁵ → O(n).
- [7,1,5,3,6,4] → 5 (buy 1, sell 6). [7,6,4,3,1] → 0.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ By hand: walking day by day, I remember the cheapest price so far. Each day I ask "if I sold today, what would I make?".
✍️ Hard part: the buy must come **before** the sell — so the max minus the min of the whole array is wrong.
✍️ Edges: prices only fall → 0; one day → 0.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** All pairs i < j. O(n²).
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: for each sell day j, scanning all earlier days for the minimum.
✍️ ↳ Unlock: "recomputing something that changed a little" — the minimum of days 0..j−1 is the minimum of days 0..j−2 plus one more day.
✍️ **2. Optimal.** Keep minSoFar; profit today = price − minSoFar. O(n), O(1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Remember the first price as the cheapest so far; best profit 0.
✍️ 2. For each later day: compute today's price minus the cheapest so far; update the best profit.
✍️ 3. Then update the cheapest so far with today's price.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   minSoFar = p[0]; best = 0
LOOP    for j in 1..n-1
UPDATE    best = max(best, p[j] - minSoFar)     sell today
          minSoFar = min(minSoFar, p[j])        today becomes a buy option
RETURN  best
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) time, O(1) space.
✍️ Max − min of the whole array is wrong when the min comes after the max ([7, 1] → 0, not 6).

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ "Best pair i < j" where the score is f(j) − g(i) → keep the best g so far.
✍️ This is the root of the stock family; adding rules (cooldown, fees, k trades) turns it into a state-machine DP.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Unlimited transactions* (LeetCode 122): sum every positive day-to-day increase.
- *At most two transactions / k transactions / cooldown / fee:* state machine DP (Day 29, [[dp-state-machine]]).
- *Return the buy and sell days.* Remember the index of minSoFar when best improves.

siblings.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
siblings.maps: With unlimited trades, every upward step can be captured — sum all positive differences.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Unlimited buy/sell (hold at most one share at a time). Maximum total profit.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Any profitable trade from i to j equals the sum of the daily increases between them, and taking every positive daily increase is never worse. Greedy O(n). (State-machine DP also works: hold/cash.)

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ For each day after the first, add max(0, today − yesterday).

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
profit = 0
for i in 1..n-1: profit += max(0, p[i] - p[i-1])
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ A long rise = a chain of daily rises, so greedy capture is safe. With fees or cooldowns that breaks → DP ([[dp-state-machine#family]]).

siblings.title: Maximum Difference Between Increasing Elements
siblings.maps: Exactly the stock problem, except "no profit" returns −1 and the difference must be strictly positive.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Max a[j] − a[i] with i < j and a[i] < a[j]; −1 if none.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Min so far; only count strictly positive differences.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Track the minimum; when a[j] > min, update the answer; then fold a[j] into the minimum.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
mn = a[0]; ans = -1
for j in 1..n-1: if a[j] > mn: ans = max(ans, a[j]-mn); mn = min(mn, a[j])
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Read the "no answer" convention carefully: 0 vs −1 changes the initialisation.

siblings.title: Best Sightseeing Pair
siblings.maps: Score a[i] + i + a[j] − j splits into (a[i] + i) + (a[j] − j) → keep the best (a[i] + i) so far.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Maximise a[i] + a[j] + i − j over i < j.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Brute O(n²). Split the score into a part depending only on i and a part only on j; for each j the best i is the max of (a[i] + i) so far.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Keep bestLeft = max(a[i] + i); at each j, candidate = bestLeft + a[j] − j; then update bestLeft with a[j] + j.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
bestLeft = a[0] + 0; ans = 0
for j in 1..n-1: ans = max(ans, bestLeft + a[j] - j); bestLeft = max(bestLeft, a[j] + j)
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ If a pair score separates into f(i) + g(j), keep the best f(i) so far ([[kad-min-so-far#variations]]).

drill.title: Sum of All Odd Length Subarrays
drill.statement: Add up the sums of every contiguous subarray whose length is odd.
drill.approach: With prefix sums, each odd-length subarray sum is O(1) → O(n²) total. O(n) trick: element i appears in ((i+1)(n−i)+1)/2 odd-length subarrays; sum a[i] × that count.
drill.trigger: "sum over many subarrays" → prefix sums, or count how many subarrays each element belongs to.
drill.details:
**Task.** Consider every contiguous subarray whose length is odd (1, 3, 5, …). Return the sum of all their sums.

**Input:** an integer array `arr`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 100; 1 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 1000. Follow-up: O(n).

**Example:** `[1, 4, 2, 5, 3]` → `58`. The length-1 subarrays add up to 15. The length-3 ones are 7, 11 and 10, so 28. The length-5 one is 15. 15 + 28 + 15 = 58.

drill.title: Find the Pivot Integer
drill.statement: Find x in 1..n such that 1 + … + x equals x + … + n, or −1.
drill.approach: Left = x(x+1)/2, right = total − left + x; scan x, or solve x² = n(n+1)/2 directly.
drill.trigger: "sum on the left equals sum on the right" → prefix sum + total (Pivot Index).
drill.details:
**Task.** Given a positive integer n, find the integer x with 1 ≤ x ≤ n such that the sum 1 + 2 + … + x equals the sum x + (x+1) + … + n. Return x, or −1 if there is none. There is at most one such x.

**Input:** an integer `n`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `n = 8` → `6` (1+…+6 = 21 = 6+7+8). `n = 1` → `1`. `n = 4` → `-1`.

drill.title: Maximum Score After Splitting a String
drill.statement: Split a binary string into two non-empty parts; score = zeros in the left part + ones in the right part. Return the best score.
drill.approach: Count all ones first; walk split points keeping zeros-so-far and ones-so-far; score = zerosLeft + (totalOnes − onesLeft). Keep both parts non-empty.
drill.trigger: "split into left and right, score each side" → one running prefix and one total.
drill.details:
**Task.** A string of 0s and 1s is cut into a non-empty left part and a non-empty right part. The score is the number of 0s in the left part plus the number of 1s in the right part. Return the best score over all possible cuts.

**Input:** a binary string `s`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 500.

**Example:** `"011101"` → `5`. Cutting after the first character gives `"0"` + `"11101"`: one zero plus four ones. `"00111"` → `5`.

drill.title: Number of Ways to Split Array
drill.statement: Count split points where the sum of the left part is at least the sum of the right part (both parts non-empty).
drill.pattern_name: Prefix sum + total, in long long
drill.approach: Total first; running left sum; at each split i (0..n−2) check left ≥ total − left. Sums up to 10¹⁰ → long long.
drill.trigger: "left sum vs right sum at every split" → running prefix + total.
drill.details:
**Task.** A split at index i (0 ≤ i < n − 1) divides the array into `nums[0..i]` and `nums[i+1..n−1]`, so both parts are non-empty. It is valid when the left part's sum is at least the right part's sum. Count the valid splits.

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 10⁵; −10⁵ ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[10, 4, -8, 7]` → `2`. The splits give 10 vs 3 (valid), 14 vs −1 (valid) and 6 vs 7 (not valid).

drill.title: Maximum Number of Balloons
drill.statement: Using each letter of a text at most once, how many copies of the word "balloon" can be formed?
drill.approach: Count letters of the text; answer = min(b, a, l/2, o/2, n).
drill.trigger: "how many times can a word be built from these letters" → counts divided by the word's own counts.
drill.details:
**Task.** You may use each character of `text` at most once. How many complete copies of the word `"balloon"` can you form?

**Input:** a string `text`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 10⁴; lowercase letters only.

**Example:** `"nlaebolko"` → `1`. `"loonbalxballpoon"` → `2`. `"leetcode"` → `0`.

cs_core.subject: OOP
cs_core.title: Polymorphism — compile time and run time

sections.title: Concept
sections.body:
✍️ **Polymorphism** = one interface, many behaviours: the same call does different things depending on the type.
✍️ **Compile-time (static)**: function overloading (same name, different parameters) and operator overloading; templates. Resolved by the compiler.
✍️ **Run-time (dynamic)**: a base-class pointer/reference calls a `virtual` function, and the **derived** class's override runs. Resolved at run time through the **vtable** (a per-class table of function pointers; each object stores a hidden pointer to its class's vtable).
✍️ Without `virtual`, the base version runs even if the object is derived (static binding).

sections.title: C++ example
Interview questions
sections.body:
✍️ **Q: Overloading vs overriding?** Overloading: same name, different parameter lists, same scope, compile time. Overriding: derived class redefines a base `virtual` function with the same signature, run time.
✍️ **Q: Why must a base class destructor be virtual?** `delete basePtr` on a derived object would otherwise call only the base destructor → the derived part leaks (undefined behaviour).
✍️ **Q: What is a vtable / vptr?** Each class with virtual functions has a vtable of function pointers; each object has a hidden vptr pointing to its class's vtable; a virtual call looks up the function through it.
- **Q: What is object slicing?** Assigning a derived object to a base object **by value** copies only the base part; virtual calls then use the base version. Use pointers/references to keep polymorphism.
- **Q: Can you overload by return type only?** No.

micro.title: Prefix sums and Kadane — subarrays without re-adding

sections.title: Micro-theory (10 minutes)
sections.body:
Day 1's running sum comes back with two superpowers.

✍️ **Prefix sums.** Store every running total in `pre` (with a leading 0). Any range sum is `pre[r+1] − pre[l]` in O(1). Draw the boundary picture once ([[ps-prefix-sum-basics#index-convention]]).
✍️ **Prefix sum + hash map.** "Subarray sum = k" means "two prefixes differ by k" — that is Two Sum on prefix sums. Seed the map with `{0: 1}` ([[ps-prefix-sum-hashmap#seed]]).
✍️ **Why not a sliding window?** Negative numbers make window sums non-monotone ([[sw-monotonicity-requirement#counterexample]]).
✍️ **Kadane.** Best subarray *ending here* = max(x, best ending at the previous index + x) ([[kad-kadane#idea]]). And its cousin: for "buy then sell", the best buy day is the minimum so far ([[kad-min-so-far#idea]]).
- Sums get big → `long long` ([[cpp-integer-overflow#where]]).

sections.title: Pattern card
sections.body:
✍️ PREFIX SUM — `pre[0]=0; pre[i+1]=pre[i]+a[i]`; sum(l..r) = pre[r+1] − pre[l].
✍️ PREFIX + MAP — trigger "count subarrays with sum k" (negatives ok). cnt{0:1}; ans += cnt[run−k]; cnt[run]++.
✍️ KADANE — cur = max(x, cur+x); best = max(best, cur); init with a[0].
✍️ MIN SO FAR — profit = x − minSoFar; then minSoFar = min(minSoFar, x).
